name: The Hadley Cell
statement: Warm air rises at the equator, sinks in the subtropics, and returns as the trade winds.
statementAccent: rises at the equator, sinks in the subtropics
meaning: The Hadley cell is a global-scale, thermally direct atmospheric convection cell in which warm, moist air rises near the equator, flows poleward high in the atmosphere, descends in the subtropics around thirty degrees north and south, and returns toward the equator near the surface, where the returning flow, deflected by Earth's rotation, forms the trade winds. There is one Hadley cell in each hemisphere, meeting near the equatorial rain belt. It is the most prominent and consistent of the circulation cells and a foundation of Earth's climate zones.
mechanism: Intense equatorial heating makes moist air rise, cool, and shed its moisture as heavy tropical rain, feeding rainforests. The now-dry air flows poleward aloft and descends in the subtropics, where sinking air warms and suppresses cloud, producing subtropical high-pressure belts and the world's great deserts. The surface return flow toward the equator is turned by the Coriolis effect into the easterly trade winds, which converge at the rising branch. Hadley's own insight invoked Earth's rotation to explain the trades' easterly direction, prefiguring the Coriolis effect, though he used the wrong conservation law and underestimated the deflection.

examples.text: The reliable easterly surface winds that carried sailing ships across the tropical oceans are the low-level branch of the Hadley circulation, turned westward by Earth's rotation.
The Sahara, Arabian, Australian, and Kalahari deserts sit beneath the descending, drying subtropical high-pressure belt of the Hadley cell's sinking branch.
The heavy equatorial rains of the rising branch mark the intertropical convergence zone, whose seasonal migration over land drives monsoon systems.

variants.name: The three-cell circulation
variants.text: The Hadley cell in the tropics, the thermally indirect Ferrel cell in mid-latitudes, and the Polar cell, which together organise the trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies.

variants.name: Hadley-cell widening
variants.text: The observed and projected poleward expansion of the Hadley cells under climate change, which could push the subtropical dry zones toward the Mediterranean and the southwestern United States.

whyItMatters: The Hadley cell is foundational to understanding the latitudinal pattern of global climate, why the equator is wet, the subtropics dry, and where the major wind belts and rainforest and desert bands lie. It underpins how we explain global wind patterns, the distribution of precipitation, and the poleward transport of heat, and it is the first-order framework taught for the general circulation of the atmosphere. Its poleward expansion under warming carries direct consequences for the world's dry subtropical regions.

working.text: trace air rising at the equator, sinking near thirty degrees, and returning as the trades to explain tropical and subtropical climate.
attribute the subtropical deserts and high-pressure belts to the cell's descending, drying branch.
note that the cells are expanding poleward under warming, which may shift subtropical dry zones toward higher latitudes.

limits: The single-cell, symmetric picture is an idealisation. The real circulation is seasonal, since the rain belt and the cells migrate with the Sun and the winter-hemisphere cell is stronger and broader, and it is zonally asymmetric, modified by continents, oceans, and monsoons, so the zonal-mean cell is a statistical average rather than a literal ring. Evidence indicates the Hadley cells have been expanding poleward, on the order of a fraction of a degree of latitude per decade since about 1980 and larger in the Southern Hemisphere, linked in part to greenhouse gases, though exact rates and attribution remain debated.
misreadings: Hadley air does not rise at the equator and sink at the pole; it sinks in the subtropics near thirty degrees, and a single equator-to-pole cell is unstable on a rotating planet, which is why there are three cells per hemisphere. Hadley did not correctly derive the Coriolis effect; he anticipated it but used linear rather than angular momentum, underestimating the deflection about twofold. Halley was not simply wrong: he correctly identified solar heating, and Hadley added the rotational deflection needed for wind direction. And the cell boundaries are not fixed at exactly thirty and sixty degrees but shift seasonally and are moving poleward.
origin: Named after George Hadley, an English scientist trained in law, who in 1735 proposed the circulation to explain the trade winds in a paper to the Royal Society, improving on Edmond Halley's 1686 solar-heating account by invoking Earth's rotation.
